changes.before: Implement orderedNotes(notes). Match the worked contract and the changed-input checks without modifying the supplied input values.
changes.after: Sort by creation value, then use the ID to break ties.

before: Pagination needs predictable ordering. When two records share a creation value, an identity tie-breaker gives them a defined order.
This exercise is a small pure JavaScript model. Its inputs are supplied directly; it does not receive live HTTP requests, operate a database, or deploy a service.
[...notes] copies the array before sort changes it. The first subtraction orders by created. A zero result makes || choose the identity comparison. Records are assumed to have distinct integer IDs.

Read the function call orderedNotes([{"id":2,"created":10},{"id":1,"created":10}]) from the inside out: the arguments supply the inputs, orderedNotes runs the body once, and return sends its result back to the caller. console.log displays that result; it does not change it.
Two notes have the same created value. Which field decides their order? The second comparison orders tied records by ID. This avoids relying on input arrival order.
after: Pagination means showing a long list in smaller pages. The list needs a predictable order. When two notes have the same creation value, use their IDs to decide which comes first.
sort changes the array it receives. [...notes] makes a new array first, so sorting it leaves the original array's order unchanged.
The comparison function subtracts b.created from a.created. A negative result puts a first; a positive result puts b first. Zero means these creation values match.
When the first subtraction is zero, || uses a.id - b.id. That orders tied notes by increasing ID. This exercise assumes numeric creation values and distinct integer IDs.
Complete orderedNotes(notes). Return a new array ordered by created, then by id for ties. Keep the original array and its note fields unchanged. The array copy still refers to the same note objects.
